doc.title: Cedar Walton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Dillard University and a Columbia Records digression
title: The money: $7,500 flat plus $1,500 per arrangement
summary: At Brower's prompting Walton reveals Columbia paid $7,500 flat plus $1,500 per arrangement, about nineteen thousand for one project, with continuing publishing royalties.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Do you care to talk about the dollars and cents of it? I mean, you said, "Well, I didn't tell 'em." What, you know …
Well, how much was I makin'? [laughs]
Yes, I mean, 'cause this gets, this gets to the, it speaks to the economics of the business at that time, and I want to follow this line of thought.

Okay. Uh, for that period in, in, in, uh my life, uh, which was in the '70s – '70s slash '80s. Yeah, uh … So you got, it encompasses the '70s and the '80s, uh …. Well, let's see here; it might say so on here. But these amounts that I'm about to reveal [laughs] were uh, flat pay was $7,500 just, without even going in the studio. Every uh, arrangement was $1,500. I found that out, I said, "What?!" So my pen got … I would write, I would, [general laughter] my pen got busy. [laughs] So I guess uh, I'm a confessed um … What do you call all those people who love money? A money-lover? No, no. [laughs] You know what I mean, uh, this kind of society.
Capitalist?
Capitalist. I'm a self-confessed capitalist. At least I was then. So uh, now I've moved on, you know. [laughs] But we're not talkin' about now; we're talkin' about then.
So you are, are you a Democratic Socialist now?
I don't know what I am. [Wait?] … [laughs] Well yeah, uh, a Dem…Democratic Socialist, yeah. [laughs]
So a project could be fifteen to twenty thousand dollars.
Uh, I guess if you do the amount loosely, yeah.
I know you did more precisely.
No, I didn't, I didn't even do anything, just, just you know, have a mail box. [laughs] But uh, yeah, but that was pretty good [inaudible]. Let me see, that's eight songs on here, only
one of 'em not mine. I uh, uh, let the bass player, the bass player had a pretty good tune, but I orchestrated it so that was … so if you … Eight times 1,500. Hm.
Twelve.
Huh?
That'd be twelve.
Okay, twelve and then the seventy-five for flat rate, uh…
Gets you to nineteen.

Yeah. Let me see, I can't think of anything else. Well, of course, the uh, well, if you wanna go into the box of uh, Harry Fox, later on, continuously, you see … wherever it's played on the radio, uh, television. Uh, I'll give you an example.
[inaudible]
Yeah, it, it adds up even, you know, it's uh, perpetual. I think that's the word. In pa, pa, perpetuity.
Perpetuity.
Yeah. [laughs] So uh, so you got two of them, man, that's not bad. Even Freddie Hubbard would come in and do a guest solo on one of these …
